source_text: Ὡς δὲ οἱ πολλοὶ ἄνθρωποι οἱ καθέλκοντες τὴν ναῦν οὐ πολλὰ αἴτια λέγοιντ’ ἄν, ἀλλ’ ἐκ πολλῶν αἴτιον ἕν (οὐκ ἔστι γὰρ αἴτιος ἕκαστος τοῦ καθέλκεσθαι τὴν ναῦν, ἀλλὰ σὺν τοῖς ἄλλοις), οὕτω καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία πρὸς κατάληψιν τῆς ἀληθείας, ζήτησις οὖσα ἀληθείας, συλλαμβάνεται, οὐκ αἰτία οὖσα καταλήψεως, σὺν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις αἰτία καὶ συνεργός. τάχα δὲ καὶ τὸ συναίτιον αἴτιον. ὡς δὲ, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ εὐδαιμονεῖν, αἴτιαι τυγχάνουσιν αἱ ἀρεταὶ πλείονες ὑπάρχουσαι. καὶ ὡς τοῦ θερμαίνεσθαι ὅ τε ἥλιος τό τε πῦρ βαλανεῖόν τε καὶ ἐσθής, οὕτω μιᾶς οὔσης τῆς ἀληθείας πολλὰ τὰ συλλαμβανόμενα πρὸς ζήτησιν αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ εὕρεσις δἰ υἱοῦ. εἰ γοῦν σκοποῖμεν, μία κατὰ δύναμίν ἐστιν ἡ ἀρετή, ταύτην δὲ συμβέβηκεν τούτοις μὲν τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐγγενομένην λέγεσθαι φρόνησιν, ἐν τούτοις δὲ σωφροσύνην, ἐν τούτοις δὲ ἀνδρείαν ἢ δικαιοσύνην. ἀνὰ τὸν αὐτὸν οὖν λόγον, καὶ μιᾶς οὔσης ἀληθείας, ἐν γεωμετρίᾳ μὲν γεωμετρίας ἀλήθεια, ἐν μουσικῇ δὲ μουσικῆς, κἀν φιλοσοφίᾳ τῇ ὀρθῇ Ἑλληνικὴ εἴη ἂν ἀλήθεια. μόνη δὲ ἡ κυρία αὕτη ἀλήθεια ἀπαρεγχείρητος, ἢν παρὰ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ παιδευόμεθα. τοῦτόν φαμεν τὸν τρόπον μιᾶς καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς δραχμῆς τῷ μὲν ναυκλήρῳ δοθείσης λέγεσθαι ναῦλον, τῷ δὲ τελώνῃ τέλος καὶ ἐνοίκιον μὲν τῶ σταθμούχῳ, μισθὸν δὲ τῷ διδασκάλῳ καὶ τῶ πιπράσκοντι ἀρραβῶνα. ἑκάστη δὲ εἴτε ἀρετὴ εἴτε καὶ ἀλήθεια συνωνύμως καλουμένη μόνου τοῦ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ἀποτελέσματός ἐστιν αἰτία. κατὰ σύγχρησιν δὲ τούτων γίνεται τὸ εὐδαιμόνως ζῆν (μὴ γὰρ δὴ εὐδαιμονῶμεν πρὸς τὰ ὀνόματα), ὅταν τὸν ὀρθὸν βίον εὐδαιμονίαν λέγωμεν καὶ εὐδαίμονα τὸν κεκοσμημένον τὴν ψυχὴν ἐναρέτως. εἰ δὲ καὶ πόρρωθεν συλλαμβάνεται φιλοσοφία πρὸς τὴν ἀληθείας εὕρεσιν, κατὰ διαφόρους ἐπιβολὰς διατείνουσα ἐπὶ τὴν προσεχῶς ἁπτομένην τῆς ἀληθείας τὴν καθ’ ἡμᾶς εἴδησιν, ἀλλὰ συλλαμβάνεταί γε τῶ λογικῶς ἐπιχειρεῖν ἐσπουδακότι ἀνθάπτεσθαι γνώσεως. χωρίζεται δὲ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ ἀλήθεια τῆς καθ’ ἡμᾶς, εἰ καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μετείληφεν ὀνόματος. καὶ μεγέθει γνώσεως καὶ ἀποδείξει κυριωτέρᾳ καὶ θεία δυνάμει καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις· θεοδίδακτοι γὰρ ἡμεῖς, ἱερὰ ὄντως, γράμματα παρὰ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ παιδευόμενοι· ἔνθεν οὐδ’ ὡσαύτως κινοῦσι τὰς ψυχάς, ἀλλὰ διαφόρῳ διδασκαλίᾳ. εἰ δὲ καὶ διαστέλλεσθαι ἡμᾶς διὰ τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας δεήσει, συναίτιον τὴν φιλοσοφίαν καὶ συνεργὸν λέγοντες τῆς ἀληθοῦς καταλήψεως, ζήτησιν οὖσαν ἀληθείας, προπαιδείαν αὐτὴν ὁμολογήσομεν τοῦ γνωστικοῦ οὐκ αἴτιον τιθέμενοι τὸ συναίτιον οὐδὲ μὴν τὸ συνεργὸν συνεκτικὸν οὐδ’ ὡς οὗ οὐκ ἄνευ τὴν φιλοσοφίαν, ἐπεὶ σχεδὸν οἱ πάντες ἄνευ τῆς ἐγκυκλίου παιδείας καὶ φιλοσοφίας τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς, οἳ δὲ καὶ ἄνευ γραμμάτων, τῇ θείᾳ καὶ βαρβάρῳ κινηθέντες φιλοσοφίᾳ, δυνάμει τὸν περὶ θεοῦ διὰ πίστεως παρειλήφαμεν λόγον, αὐτουργῷ σοφίᾳ πεπαιδευμένοι. ὃ δὲ μεθ’ ἑτέρου ποιεῖ, ἀτελὲς ὂν καθ’ αὑτὸ ἐνεργεῖν, συνεργόν φαμεν καὶ συναίτιον ἀπὸ τοῦ δὺν αἰτίῳ αἴτιον ὑπάρχειν ἢ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑτέρῳ συνελθὸν αἴτιον γίγνεσθαι ὠνομασμένον, καθ’ ἑαυτὸ δὲ μὴ δύνασθαι τὸ ἀποτέλεσμα τὸ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν παρέχειν. καίτοι καὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ἐδικαίου ποτὲ καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία τοὺς Ἕλληνας, οὐκ εἰς τὴν καθόλου δὲ δικαιοσύνην, εἰς ἣν εὑρίσκεται συνεργός(καθάπερ καὶ ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ δεύτερος βαθμὸς τῷ εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον ἀνιόντι καὶ γραμματιστὴς τῷ φιλοσοφήσοντι), οὐδ’ ὡς κατὰ τὴν ἀφαίρεσιν αὐτῆς ἤτοι ἐλλείπειν τῷ καθόλου λόγῳ ἢ ἀναιρεῖσθαι τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἐπεὶ ἡ ὄψις συμβάλλεται καὶ ἡ ἀκοὴ καὶ ἡ φωνὴ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν, νοῦς δὲ ὁ γνωρίζων αὐτὴν προσφυῶς. ἀλλὰ τῶν συνεργῶν τὰ μὲν πλείονα, τὰ δ’ ἐλάσσονα προσφέρεται δύναμιν. ἡ γοῦν σαφήνεια συνεργεῖ πρὸς τὴν παράδοσιν τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ ἡ διαλεκτικὴ πρὸς τὸ μὴ ὑποπίπτειν ταῖς κατατρεχούσαις αἱρέσεσιν. αὐτοτελὴς μὲν οὖν καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς ἡ κατὰ τὸν σωτῆρα διδασκαλία, δύναμις οὖσα καὶ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ, προσιοῦσα δὲ φιλοσοφία ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ οὐ δυνατωτέραν ποιεῖ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἀλλ’ ἀδύνατον παρέχουσα τὴν κατ’ αὐτῆς σοφιστικὴν ἐπιχείρησιν καὶ διακρουομένη τὰς δολερὸς κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπιβουλὰς φραγμὸς οἰκείως εἴρηται καὶ θριγκὸς εἶναι τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος. καὶ ἣ μὲν ὡς ἄρτος ἀναγκαία πρὸς τὸ ζῆν, ἡ κατὰ τὴν πίστιν ἀλήθεια· ἡ προπαιδεία δὲ προσοψήματι ἔοικεν καὶ τραγήματι, δείπνου δὲ λήγοντος γλυκὺ τρωγάλιον κατὰ τὸν Θηβαῖον Πίνδαρον. ἄντικρυς δὲ ἐξεῖπεν ἡ γραφή· πανουργότερος ἔσται ἄκακος συνίων, ὁ δὲ σοφὸς δέξεται γνῶσιν. καὶ ὁ μὲν ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ λαλῶν τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἰδίαν ζητεῖ, φησὶν ὁ κύριος, ὁ δὲ ζητῶν τὴν δόξαν τοῦ πέμψαντος αὐτὸν ἀληθής ἐστι καὶ ἀδικία οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ. ἔμπαλιν οὖν ἀδικεῖ ὁ σφετερισάμενος τὰ βαρβάρων καὶ ὡς ἴδια αὐχῶν, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δόξαν αὔξων καὶ ψευδόμενος τὴν ἀλήθειαν. οὗτος κλέπτης ὑπὸ τῆς γραφῆς εἴρηται. φησὶ γοῦν· υἱέ, μὴ γίνου ψεύστης· ὁδηγεῖ γὰρ τὸ ψεῦσμα πρὸς τὴν κλοπήν. ἤδη δὲ ὁ κλέπτης ὅπερ ὑφελόμενος ἔχει ἀληθῶς κἂν χρυσίον ᾖ κἂν ἄργυρος κἂν λόγος κἂν δόγμα. ἐκ μέρους τοίνυν, ἃ κεκλόφασιν, ἀληθῆ μέν, στοχαστικῶς δὲ καὶ ταῖς τῶν λόγων ἀνάγκαις ἴσασι. μαθητευθέντες οὖν καταληπτικῶς ἐπιγνώσονται.
pass_a_gloss: As the many people who pull the ship do not give many reasons, but one reason from many, for the ship is not pulled by each one individually, but together with the others, so also philosophy, being a search for truth, is taken hold of, not being a cause of attainment, but together with other things it is a cause and a co-worker. Perhaps also the co-causal is a cause. Just as, since there is one happiness, the many virtues are causes. And just as the sun and fire and bath and clothing warm, so also, since there is one truth, many things are taken hold of for the search of it, and the discovery is through the Son. If then we consider, virtue is one in power, but it is called prudence in these things, and temperance in these, and courage or justice in these. In the same way, since there is one truth, in geometry it is geometric truth, in music it is musical truth, and in correct Greek philosophy it would be truth. But the only sovereign truth is that which is imparted by the Son of God. We say that in the same way, one drachma given to the shipowner is called naulon, to the tax collector it is called telos, and to the teacher it is called misthos. Each virtue or truth, so called, is a cause of its own effect. By the use of these things, living happily comes about, not because we are happy with names, but when we call the correct life happiness and the one who has adorned his soul with virtue happy. If indeed philosophy is taken hold of from afar for the discovery of truth, extending through various efforts to the knowledge of truth that is near to us, but it is taken hold of by one who logically endeavors to attain knowledge. The Greek truth is separated from our truth, even if it has shared the same name. And it is greater in knowledge and demonstration and divine power and the like, for we are taught by God, truly holy writings from the Son of God. Whence it does not move our souls in the same way, but with different teaching. If indeed we must distinguish ourselves from those who love disputes, saying that philosophy is a co-causal and co-worker for the true attainment, being a search for truth, we will confess it as a propaedeutic, not placing the co-causal as a cause, nor indeed the co-worker as a holder, nor as one without which philosophy is not possible, since almost all people, without the cyclical education and Greek philosophy, and some even without writings, having been moved by the divine and barbarian philosophy, have received the word about God through faith, being self-taught in wisdom. What works with another, being incomplete in itself, we call a co-worker and co-causal, from the fact that it has a cause or becomes a cause when combined with another, but in itself it is not able to provide the true effect. Although philosophy has justified the Greeks in themselves, not in general justice, in which it is found to be a co-worker, just as the first and second step are for the one ascending to the upper level, and the grammarian is for the one philosophizing, not as if the absence of it would lack the general word or destroy the truth, since sight and hearing and voice contribute to the truth, and the mind knows it intimately. But of the co-workers, some contribute more power, others less. Clarity co-operates for the transmission of truth, and dialectic for not falling into the heresies that are pursued. The teaching according to the Savior is self-sufficient and without need, being the power and wisdom of God, but Greek philosophy, when added, does not make the truth more powerful, but rather, providing its own sophistical effort, and warding off the cunning plots against the truth, it is said to be a fence and a hedge of the vineyard. And the truth according to faith is like bread, necessary for living, but philosophy is like a prologue and a dessert, a sweet after-dinner snack, according to the Theban Pindar. But the scripture has spoken clearly: the cunning person will be innocent, understanding, and the wise person will accept knowledge. And the one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, the Lord says, but the one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true and there is no unrighteousness in him. On the contrary, the one who has seized the things of the barbarians and boasts them as his own, increasing his own glory and lying about the truth, is unjust. This person is called a thief by the scripture. For it says: do not become a liar, my son, for lying leads to theft. Already the thief, what he has stolen, truly has, whether it is gold or silver or word or doctrine. Therefore, from the part that they have stolen, they know the true things, but in a conjectural way and with the necessities of words. Having been taught in a attainable way, they will recognize intimately.

pass_b_english: Just as the many people who pull a ship do not offer many reasons for its movement but one reason arising from many — since no single person pulls the ship alone, but each does so together with the others — so also philosophy, being a search for truth, is taken hold of not as a cause of attainment in itself, but as a cause and co-worker together with other things. Perhaps the co-causal is also a cause. Just as, because there is one happiness, the many virtues are causes, and just as the sun, fire, a bath, and clothing all warm, so also, since there is one truth, many things are taken hold of for the search for it, and the discovery comes through the Son. If we consider the matter, virtue is one in power, yet it happens to be called prudence in these matters, temperance in those, and courage or justice in others. In the same way, since truth is one, in geometry it is geometric truth, in music it is musical truth, and in correct Greek philosophy it would be Greek truth. But the only sovereign truth, which is unerring, is that by which we are educated by the Son of God. We say that in the same way a single drachma given to the shipowner is called fare, to the tax collector it is called tax, to the innkeeper it is called rent, to the teacher it is called wages, and to the seller it is called earnest money. Each virtue or truth, so named synonymously, is a cause only of its own proper effect. By the combined use of these things comes living happily — for we are not made happy by names — when we call the right life happiness and call happy the person who has adorned his soul with virtue. Even if philosophy is taken hold of from afar for the discovery of truth, extending through various efforts to the knowledge of truth that touches us closely, still it is taken hold of by the one who logically strives to kindle knowledge. Greek truth is separated from our truth, even though it has shared the same name. Ours is greater in knowledge, in more authoritative demonstration, in divine power, and in such things; for we are taught by God, truly holy writings, educated by the Son of God. Hence it does not move souls in the same way, but with a different teaching. If we must distinguish ourselves from those who love disputes, saying that philosophy is a co-causal and co-worker for the true attainment, being a search for truth, we will confess it as a propaedeutic for the knowledge that comes through faith, not positing the co-causal as a cause, nor the co-worker as a sustainer, nor as that without which philosophy would be impossible — since nearly all, without the cyclical education and Greek philosophy, and some even without letters, having been moved by the divine and barbarian philosophy, have received the word concerning God through faith, educated by self-acting wisdom. What works with another, being incomplete in itself to act alone, we call a co-worker and co-causal, because it has power as a cause from the one that is a cause, or becomes a cause when joined with another, but in itself is not able to supply the true effect. Even so, philosophy once justified the Greeks in themselves, not with respect to universal justice, in which it is found to be a co-worker, just as the first and second step are for the one ascending to the upper room, and the grammarian is for the one who will philosophize — not as if its absence would make the universal account lacking or would destroy the truth, since sight and hearing and voice contribute to truth, and the mind is the one that knows it intimately. But among co-workers, some contribute more power, others less. Clarity co-operates for the transmission of truth, and dialectic for not yielding to the heresies that run their course. The teaching according to the Savior is self-sufficient and without need, being the power and wisdom of God; but Greek philosophy, when added, does not make the truth more powerful — rather, by providing an impossibility for the sophistical attempt against it and by warding off the cunning plots against the truth, it has aptly been called a fence and a hedge of the vineyard. And the truth according to faith is like bread, necessary for life; but the propaedeutic is like a side dish and a dessert, a sweet after-dinner treat at the end of the feast, according to the Theban Pindar. But Scripture has spoken plainly: "The innocent who understands will become shrewd, and the wise will accept knowledge" (Proverbs 10:9). And the one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, the Lord says, but the one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him. On the contrary, the one who has seized the things of the barbarians and boasts of them as his own, increasing his own glory and lying about the truth, acts unjustly. This person is called a thief by Scripture. For it says: "My son, do not become a liar, for lying leads to theft." Already the thief, what he has stolen, truly possesses, whether it is gold or silver or word or doctrine. Therefore, from the part that they have stolen, they know true things, but conjecturally and according to the necessities of words. Having been discipled in an attainable way, they will recognize them intimately.
